item.title: You're a Perfectionist. They're Not. Can You Make it Work?
item.description:
ADHD

You're a Perfectionist. They're Not. Can You Make it Work?

Personal Perspective: Helping couples bridge signature differences.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectionists seek order for safety; non-perfectionists prioritize differently, not out of spite.
  • Recognizing your differences and not personalizing conflict helps reduce relationship friction.
  • Mutual respect and regular check-ins foster better understanding of each other’s needs.
Source: Getty images/Unsplash

You might initially think it can't work—after all, what could be more opposite than these two extremes?

Actually, this isn't an unusual combination in couples—mostly because there are a lot of people who experience, to one degree or another, these two tendencies. But can they find happiness together with such opposite needs?

I remember sitting with a certain couple in my practice: he had a tendency toward being scattered, unaware, and she was a perfectionist. She lived for maintaining order and cleanliness—to a fault. For her, wiping the counter had its own system; dishes had to be loaded into the dishwasher in a certain order. Her husband, on the other hand, had the perspective that such things just didn’t matter—after all, no one was going to die—and couldn’t understand why she kept getting upset with him.

Source: Getty Images/Unsplash

She kept watching him, anticipating a crime that hadn’t yet happened; he kept watching her, wondering when she was going to snap at him over some trivial thing.

They recognized this ongoing tension and one evening, just as a game, decided to ask an AI bot whether what they were experiencing was normal. To their surprise, the answer came back with their relationship spelled out right in front of them. Yes, the bot said; this is a real thing. The tension between them around how things were done or not done, they learned, is not uncommon. It was an extremely validating experience that they brought in turn into my office for us to all talk about.

How Do You Identify Your Own Personality Tendency?

Most of us lean into one of these categories. Which are you? Maybe you, too, believe there is one correct way to load a dishwasher or sort the bills; or maybe you want to focus on something other than household tasks and don’t see the big deal with leaving a shirt on the bedroom chair. Whichever way you lean, it’s probably brought you into conflict at some point with your partner.

It’s happened to me. I totally believe there’s only one way that tasks should be done; I’m the person whisking a coaster under a glass or making sure the kitchen is spotless before I can go to bed; my husband saves his energy for his professional life—at which he excels—and isn’t particularly interested in the proper way to wipe down a counter!

Let’s look at what’s going on for each of these people:

  • The "perfectionist" individual feels safe with order: they need to feel the control and safety that an external order offers. People who are scattered evoke uneasiness in their partner's body: they feel disconnected in what they perceive as the chaos generated by the other person.
  • For the less-structured person, the details aren’t particularly important: if things are “good enough” then everything is fine. They have a difficult time coping with structure, as their minds are running about four steps ahead of wherever they are—what others perceive as chaos, they see as prioritization.

One woman puts the conflict she experiences this way: “If I have to do things his way, I get frustrated and in tears by the end of it, because our brains are just so different.” She explains how it feels: “Normal people have thoughts that they put on a shelf in their brains. And then when they want to think about something they scan the shelves and pick the thought that they want to think about. But I don't have any shelves, and my thoughts don't sit still.”

It's about feeling safe

Source: Nik/Unsplash

In an ideal world, each partner would recognize that the other isn’t doing things differently just to irritate or punish them. Each finds comfort and safety in their own way of approaching life; the challenge is in tolerating living with someone whose focus is completely different from one's own. The perfectionist could take ownership of those tasks that are important to them and be less critical when things are done differently; their partner could define areas where they’re willing to accommodate the other’s needs and places where they cannot.

I went to a funeral once where the recent widower eulogized his deceased spouse. During the eulogy, he remembered—fondly, as it were—how his wife just tossed things in the dishwasher, and he’d come in and rearrange everything after she’d loaded it. The whole room laughed.

It would be helpful for everyone to stake a step back in these fraught moments and remind themselves that their partner isn't doing anything deliberately to punish them, because it isn't personal. Perfectionist individuals need structure to soothe themselves and make them feel more comfortable. More scattered individuals are struggling with a world that feels it's going by too fast and has too much that needs doing at once.

If partners can recognize what governs the other person and not personalize the ensuing conflicts, then there's a greater chance that conflicts will diminish or at least be better handled. Creating ongoing check-ins with each other to see how things are going between them based on how they function differently in the world can help partners devise strategies that incorporate respect.

We all have tendencies one way or the other. The solution to the friction that exists when spouses are leaning in different directions on this scale is to recognize, honor, and understand your differences—and to communicate.

Source: Cord Allman/Unsplash

item.title: Feeling Her After She Died, What If I'm Not Imagining It?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Feeling Her After She Died, What If I'm Not Imagining It?

Personal Perspective: I felt something when Mom died. Is science catching up?

Posted August 11, 2026

Source: iStockphoto/Truelight

I sat beside my mother, holding her hand, knowing she was close to her last breath. I had pictured this moment many times in the past few weeks, knowing it was coming and couldn’t be stopped, but what happened next was beyond anything I’d imagined.

I felt her as she left, from the inside. The closest I can come to describing it is a hug, not the hug my mother and I shared when she was still in her body, but one beginning in my heart and radiating outward, carrying with it a rush of peace, warmth, and joy, and of being so deeply loved that I smiled. It’s a sensation I can’t rationally explain, and with it came a certainty, absolute, that everything was more than okay.

In the hours that followed, the grief came, because of course it did, but beneath it was something steadier, a current of her presence that arrived in that moment and never left. Instead of her absence defining my days, I feel her presence in a new (interior) way, and most of the time, I feel what I can only call calmer than I have any right to feel.

As a researcher and practicing clinician, I know much of the literature over the past hundred years explains experiences like mine away as projection, wishful thinking, or the mind softening an unbearable loss. But I know what I’m feeling, and over the past few years, the research has begun to offer a deeper account of consciousness and of death and of what it means to remain connected to someone who has left their body behind. And it lines up with my experience.

The Broken Radio

For more than a century, the dominant scientific view was, simply put, that the brain produces consciousness, and when the brain dies, consciousness ends. But this view has its problems, and Masi (2023) explains them neatly: In instance after instance, people with “less brain” demonstrate intact or enhanced consciousness. He cites savant abilities emerging after brain injury; patients with severe dementia suddenly gaining remarkable clarity before death; and children with massive hydrocephalus (virtually no cortical tissue) scoring well on cognitive tests. Each one is the opposite of what the brain-produces-consciousness theory would predict.

Researchers began asking, if the brain doesn’t produce consciousness, where does consciousness come from? Woollacoot and Weiler (2025), writing in the International Review of Psychiatry, examined the brain’s neural filters and offered an answer: There exists a wider consciousness, and our brains tap into it and filter it into the smaller consciousness each of us experiences. When the filters are widened through deep meditation, psychedelic states, or near-death experiences, awareness expands, and people report transcending time and space, access to information beyond the usual senses, and ego dissolution. Death is the ultimate removal of these neural filters and represents not the end of consciousness but its fullest expansion.

Woollacott and Weiler aren’t alone. Researchers Moreira-Almeida (2025) and Tallarico (2026) offer strikingly similar views, and together they make compelling arguments that consciousness is not produced by the brain, but received by it. When the brain stops, consciousness goes on, like a radio breaking but the music playing on.

Still Being With Them

Encouraged, I wondered what the latest literature might say about my sitting beside my mother’s emptied body and feeling her presence with me like a warmth.

First, it told me that my experience isn’t uncommon. Sweeney and colleagues (2026) conducted a systematic review of 14 studies involving 1,971 bereaved participants, all of whom reported after-death communications. They concluded these were “relationally meaningful experiences” that “facilitated continuing bonds with the deceased.”

But the research went further, asking if contact with the deceased could be verified. Delorme and colleagues (2013) measured EEG during sessions where mediums were given only a first name and asked questions about the deceased person. Three of four mediums scored significantly above chance on accuracy, and their mental state showed electrocortical signatures distinct from ordinary thinking, from imagination, and from recalling a known living person. When Paraná and colleagues (2019) examined a letter written by the Brazilian medium Chico Xavier, said to be written on behalf of a deceased person, all 29 objectively verifiable details in it, names, dates, and highly private events, were rated a “clear and precise fit,” leading the researchers to conclude that ordinary explanations such as fraud, chance, information leakage, and cold reading were highly unlikely.

My Mother

For a long time, my mother was afraid to die, seeing it as the final separation from everyone she’d ever loved. In the weeks prior to her death, I told her what I believe: Death is not the separation she feared, but its opposite, the raindrop falling back into the ocean, the homecoming to the largest village there is.

I believe this now more than I did then, because now I feel it. She’s not gone, not distant, simply here in a way that is more than memory and stronger than grief. She crossed over, and instead of losing her, I found her in a new way, a hug from the inside that has not ended.

That’s what the research is beginning to recognize: Mom’s consciousness wasn’t extinguished; it was liberated, freed from the neural filters that contained it in a single body. And I, still here in filtered consciousness, felt her expanding consciousness, warm and immediate, arriving from inside.

My mother is with me. I’m certain of it.
